title: UK company data: explained, connected, usable
text:
UK company data is free, large and genuinely useful — and awkward to use. It is spread across several registers, published in formats built for filing rather than analysis, and shaped by rules that are easy to misread. This site does three things: it explains what Companies House and the other UK sources publish, it connects them by showing how they join and what each adds, and it publishes tested, ready-to-use datasets built from them. Where code adds something beyond what already exists, we add it; where it doesn’t, we link to the best existing explanation instead.
This is methodology and open data, not a company-rating product. Register records can support due-diligence signals; they cannot establish that a company is trustworthy, solvent or non-fraudulent. Nothing here produces a composite score, publishes named company results, or includes personal data.

section: What this is, and is not
text:
What this is, and is not

No composite score, anywhere. The indicator pipeline records discrete, registrar-sourced facts as flags with a severity and an evidence string. Severity grades the seriousness of the recorded state, not confidence in it. There is no single number.
No named results, no personal data. The repository publishes code, methodology and synthetic fixtures only. Run outputs, officer/PSC-level data and named flag lists stay private. The published accounts datasets contain financial facts and company numbers only.
Open licence. Source data is Crown copyright, published under the Open Government Licence v3.0 and free to reuse with attribution. The OGL does not cover personal data, which is part of why personal data is removed before anything is published.

title: Companies House: what it publishes and how to get it
text:
Companies House is the UK’s register of companies: it incorporates and dissolves companies, records what they file, and publishes almost all of it. The register has been free to search and download since 2015, and it is heavily used — billions of accesses a year. For an analyst, four things matter: three free bulk data products (basic company data, the accounts archive, and the daily PSC snapshot) plus a free REST API for current, per-company detail. The important catch is that the API returns register fields but not parsed financial figures — to get numbers out of accounts you still have to download and parse the filings yourself, which is what this project does at scale.
For the low-level mechanics of each bulk product (file formats, where the historic archives live, how often they refresh), CH Guide already documents them well, and this guide links there rather than repeating them. The aim here is to explain what each source adds for analysis and where it will surprise you.

Details

What Companies House is
Companies House is an executive agency of the Department for Business and Trade. It is the registrar for companies across England & Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Historically it did very little checking of what companies filed; reforms under the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 (ECCTA) are turning it from a passive record into a register that verifies identities and can query or reject information. That transition is still rolling out, so “verified” is not yet a safe assumption for older records.

Source: deck slide 4 and its notes.
Two terms, with concrete examples:

iXBRL (“inline XBRL”): an ordinary-looking HTML accounts page in which each figure is tagged with a machine-readable name — for example <nonFraction name="Equity">12,968 tags the number 12,968 as the company’s equity. A browser shows the page; a parser reads the tags. See the accounts guide for what this means in practice.
PSC: a person with significant control — broadly, someone who owns or controls more than 25% of a company, or otherwise exerts significant influence. The daily snapshot is newline-delimited JSON, one record per line. See the PSC status page.


What it means for you. The API is the right tool for current, per-company state (status, overdue flags, insolvency links). It is the wrong tool for financials and for history: it returns no parsed numbers from accounts, and no bulk back-catalogue. That gap — API-for-state, bulk-download-plus-your-own-parser-for-financials — is the single most important thing to understand about getting data out of Companies House.

The published REST API rate limit is about 600 requests per 5 minutes per key ([Not verified] — stated from the developer docs in deck slide 4’s notes but not re-checked here; confirm against the current developer documentation). This project’s own indicator pipeline deliberately runs below that (≈500/5min) because an API key may be shared across tools — see the indicators methodology.


Why we link to CH Guide instead of repeating it
CH Guide is a thorough, well-maintained explanation of Companies House mechanics — the exact file layouts, the historic-archive pages back to 2008, the quirks of each download. Re-documenting that here would duplicate work that is already done well and would go stale faster than the original. So this guide links to CH Guide for mechanics and concentrates on the layer above it: how the sources join, what each one adds for analysis, and the pitfalls that only show up once you start using the data.

title: The accounts data: mostly balance sheets
text:
Almost every UK company must file annual accounts, and Companies House publishes the electronically filed ones as a free bulk archive. But what a company files depends on its size, and most UK companies are small or micro. Small and micro companies may file “filleted” accounts — the balance sheet and its notes only, with no profit-and-loss account. The practical result is that, for most companies, the public data has no turnover and no profit figure at all: it is, in effect, a balance-sheet dataset. Accounts are tagged in iXBRL, a format that is both human-readable in a browser and machine-readable, so the figures can be extracted at scale.
Two changes matter for anyone using this data. Size thresholds rose on 6 April 2025 (their first change since 2013), moving some companies into lighter-disclosure bands. And from April 2028, reforms will require small companies to file a profit-and-loss account — but that will not fill in the past, so anyone modelling history still works with balance-sheet-only data.

title: The accounts data: mostly balance sheets
text:
Details

Who files what
Under the Companies Act 2006, essentially every registered company must file annual accounts (private companies have nine months after the year-end). A company’s size band is set by meeting two of three tests — turnover, balance-sheet total, and average employees — over two consecutive years. From 6 April 2025 the monetary thresholds rose by roughly half:

Employees

≤ £1m

Source: deck slides 11–12 and the accounts explainer (docs/source-material/accounts-explainer.html); thresholds via Lexology summary of the 6 April 2025 change. [Checked] (official change date; figures are the published thresholds).
Filleted accounts are the defining feature. Under section 444 of the Act, small companies and micro-entities prepare full accounts for their shareholders and HMRC, but file only the balance sheet and notes with Companies House — omitting the profit-and-loss account and directors’ report. Since the overwhelming majority of UK companies are small or micro, the public dataset is, in practice, a balance-sheet dataset.

What it means for you. For most companies there is no turnover and no profit in the public data — not because the extraction missed it, but because it was never filed. One useful quirk: the average-employees note is generally treated as not a profit-and-loss note, so it usually survives filleting, which is why headcount is far better covered than any income-statement item. Credit agencies work around the missing turnover by estimating it from balance-sheet items and sector ratios (Creditsafe publicly describes an “Estimated Turnover Indicator”) — these are modelled figures, not filed ones, so treat them with care.



How it is tagged: iXBRL
iXBRL (“inline XBRL”) is an ordinary-looking HTML accounts document in which each figure is tagged with a machine-readable name. Concretely, a line that displays as “Equity 12,968” is tagged in the HTML as something like:
<ix:nonFraction name="Equity" unitRef="GBP" decimals="0">12,968</ix:nonFraction>
A browser renders “12,968”; a parser reads that the value 12,968 is Equity, in GBP. Each tag also carries a reporting period, a unit (pounds, a count, a ratio), an optional scale (for example, “thousands”), a sign, and optional dimensions (for example, creditors split into “due within one year” and “after one year”).
Tags follow FRC taxonomies — FRS 105 for micro-entities, FRS 102 (including Section 1A) for small and larger companies — which define the machine-readable name for each figure. The taxonomies are revised often, so this project targets each concept’s stable local name and reads across taxonomy generations without a version map. See the accounts guide to pitfalls for what goes wrong at the tag level.

Why the data starts in 2014. iXBRL adoption in the bulk product was gradual, not a hard cutover: roughly 0% of filings were iXBRL in 2010, rising through 2011–2013 and reaching ~97% by 2014. Earlier accounts exist on the server but are barely machine-tagged, so the dataset starts in 2014 — a coverage decision, not a limit of Companies House’s archive. Source: docs/accounts-limitations.md and deck slide 11 notes. [Checked] (project measurement).



What’s changing







When
Change




2008
Bulk accounts product begins (e-filed only)


~2014
iXBRL nearly universal in the bulk data


6 April 2025
Size thresholds raised ~50%


2025–26
Identity checks for directors and PSCs (ECCTA)


April 2028
Software-only iXBRL filing; small & micro firms must file a P&L



The 2028 reforms (Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023) will require small companies and micro-entities to file a profit-and-loss account, move all filing to commercial software in iXBRL, and remove the filleted/abridged options. After a pause, this was confirmed on 9 June 2026 for April 2028 (delayed from 2027), and the government has indicated small-company P&L data may be kept private rather than published. Source: ICAEW, June 2026 (deck slide 11 notes; accounts explainer). [Checked] as of June 2026 — the date has already moved once, so re-confirm before relying on it.

What it means for you. Future data will be richer, but 2028 does not fill in history: past filings stay balance-sheet-only, and any newly required small-company P&L may stay private. Anyone modelling on the historical archive must work with balance-sheet-only data for the foreseeable future.

title: Accounts dataset (WIDE & LONG, 2014–2026)
text:
This is an open, analysis-ready version of twelve years of UK company accounts, built from Companies House’s free monthly bulk archives. It comes in two tables. WIDE is one row per company per accounting period, with the core balance-sheet figures as columns — the table most people want for modelling. LONG is a fuller, personal-data-removed table — one row per fact, reaching the concepts the curated columns leave out — for anyone who needs more than WIDE. Coverage is continuous from January 2014 to August 2026 (152 monthly archives, no gaps), and both published tables contain financial facts and company numbers only — no names, addresses or other personal data. The complete as-filed archive (which does contain director names, addresses and loans) is kept private and never published; what you can download is the filtered subset described under Licence below.
The one decision you must make before using WIDE is which pivot to read: as_first_reported (what was known at the time — use this for anything predictive) or latest (includes later restatements — do not use it for prediction). Everything else on this page is about using the tables correctly: the columns, the known limitations, and the licence.

Most rows are sparse, and that is expected. A company reporting only Equity and CurrentAssets for a year genuinely filed filleted accounts without the rest — it is not a gap in the extraction. See the accounts guide.



as_first_reported vs latest
Both files share the same schema; they differ only in which filing wins each cell.

accounts-wide-as_first_reported.parquet (flagship, default). Each cell holds the value from the earliest filing that reported it — only information available at the time, no look-ahead. Use this for any predictive or point-in-time work.
accounts-wide-latest.parquet (secondary). Each cell holds the value from the most recent filing, which can include later comparative restatements of an earlier period. Do not use this for predictive work — a value can reflect information that postdates the period.

Across the full span, 9.36% of repeated (company, period, concept) values disagree between first-reported and a later filing, which is exactly why the two files are kept separate rather than collapsed into one ambiguous “current” column. Source: docs/accounts-validation-summary.md, docs/accounts-restatement-2014-2026.md.


Quickstart
The files are Parquet, so polars, pandas, DuckDB or Spark all work. row_available_yyyymm is the month by which every value in a row had been filed, which makes point-in-time filtering a single comparison. The company number below (00012345) is a placeholder — substitute a real one.
import polars as pl

wide = pl.read_parquet("accounts-wide-as_first_reported.parquet")

# one company's history (company numbers are TEXT — keep the leading zeros)
(wide
   .filter(pl.col("company") == "00012345")
   .sort("period_end"))

# only what was known as of a date: no look-ahead
wide.filter(pl.col("row_available_yyyymm") <= 202312)
Rules of thumb, each because it changes how the data should be used:

Pivot mode — as_first_reported for prediction; latest leaks the future (~9% of repeated figures differ).
Creditors — use creditors_within_one_year / creditors_after_one_year; the bare total is ~4% populated and unreliable even when present.
Employees — ~29% are GBP-tagged (median value 1.0, mostly real headcounts). The flag marks them; no value is removed. Don’t filter employees by unit.
Dashes — a dash in the accounts means nil and is stored as 0, not null.
Missing is not zero — values are never imputed, and some missingness is non-random, so decide explicitly how to handle gaps.

Source: deck slides 15–16 and notes (docs/source-material/companies-house-accounts-deck.md); see also pitfalls.


Limitations to know before modelling

Balance-sheet only for most companies (filleted filing): no turnover or profit.
Starts in 2014 — earlier bulk data is barely machine-tagged.
Some breakdowns skipped — facts in multi-member or custom (typed-member) dimensional contexts are not captured; ~38% of filings contain at least one such context (these are mostly detailed notes, not the balance-sheet totals WIDE uses).
Nine core concepts validated — the other ~4,580 concepts in LONG are captured as filed but not validated; check the source filing before relying on a rare one.
Restatements (~9%) and an employee reporting break around 2020–2021.
Non-random gaps — e.g. equity fill-rate varies by more than 10 percentage points across months.
GBP only in WIDE — non-sterling filers are excluded (kept in LONG), not converted.

Full detail and every reconciliation: docs/accounts-limitations.md. Source: deck slide 17.


Licence and personal-data policy
Contains public sector information from Companies House, licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0, free to reuse with attribution. Companies House and the UK Government do not endorse this dataset, and a derived dataset is not a complete or official representation of any company.
Both published tables are financial facts and company numbers only. WIDE carries no names, addresses or director figures. LONG applies a maintainer-approved filter: a 95-concept numeric denylist (director/officer/key-management/related-party remuneration, loans and advances) and a 17-concept non-numeric allowlist of structured fields only (dates, the registered number, filing-software name, and categorical flags) — every other non-numeric concept, including all free text, is dropped. The private, unfiltered archive that includes personal data is never published. The OGL does not cover personal data, which is part of why this split exists. Source: docs/accounts-public-long-concepts.md, docs/accounts-limitations.md.

title: The market: who sells company data, and where the value sits
text:
A market of commercial providers sells UK company data — from credit-reference agencies (Creditsafe, Dun & Bradstreet, Experian, Equifax) through research platforms (Moody’s Bureau van Dijk’s FAME, Beauhurst) to low-cost and freemium tools (Endole, Company Check, OpenCorporates, DataLedger). What they charge for is mostly not the raw data, which is free: it is cleaning, history, linking, a usable interface, scores and support. The important exception is a small private data layer — trade-payment behaviour, bank-credit data and court judgments — that is genuinely not public and carries much of the predictive power behind credit scores. So the fair summary is “most, not all”: open data plus good engineering reproduces most of the descriptive stack, but not the private layer that predicts who will not pay.
All prices below are indicative only, drawn from third-party price guides and vendor pages as summarised in the project deck (2026). They are negotiable, change often, and should be verified before quoting. Each carries a confidence label.

Much of what you pay for is convenience. Filed financials, officers and ownership are free; vendors charge for cleaning, history, linking and a usable interface.

The GIS comparison. title: Indicators: methodology
text:
Pipeline
open-company-uk validates supplied company numbers, fetches and caches raw Companies House responses, derives a wide attribute table, and applies a rule registry to create discrete flags with severity, evidence, and observation time. Cache envelopes retain retrieval metadata and content hashes, allowing derivation and scoring to be replayed without network access.

Evidence tiers

Tier 1: registrar-recorded statuses, events, and compliance facts suitable for the shipped rule registry.
Tier 2: structured but self-reported or identity-related register data that needs qualification, including officer and PSC records.

Severity
Severity grades the seriousness of the recorded state, not confidence in the record or certainty about a company. high marks serious registrar-recorded adverse states/events; medium marks material compliance failures; low marks weaker or less serious concerns; info supplies context. Summary
The evidence register is the project’s catalogue of sources — official datasets and APIs, tools and products, other countries’ registers, papers and investigations, and the governing law and licences. Its job is to keep three things separate that are easy to blur: what a source is, what it claims, and what has actually been observed or measured. Details
The register schema, update rules and discovery queue live in the repository’s literature/ directory and are summarised here. Source files: open-uk-company-research-pack.md (schema, §4), open-company-uk-source-queue-2026-08.md (the discovery queue), and companies-house-data-landscape.md (the data/attribute landscape).

What a register row records
One row per finished source, with these fields (abbreviated): register_id, source_type, title, authors_or_operator, year_or_version, jurisdiction, source_artifact, extraction_file, main_question, evidence_role, operational_proximity, access_class, main_data_or_method, outcome_or_purpose, validation_type, current_repo_relevance, future_research_relevance, actionability_now, supports_production_change, main_limit, review_status, reviewed_on, recheck_by, notes.
ID prefixes mark the kind of source: DATA- (official dataset/API/register), TOOL- (tool/product), REG- (country-register review), USE- (paper/report/investigation/repo), GOV- (law/licence/governance), METH- (method/entity-resolution/validation).

The guardrails the register enforces
The point of the register is disciplined honesty, so its update rules are strict: append-only by default; never silently change an earlier judgement (add a dated note or a superseding row); do not upgrade a claimed finding to observed or measured; an official source defines a field or access rule but does not thereby validate an analytical indicator; a vendor source supports what the vendor claims to offer, not independent effectiveness; and keep data-existence, capability, observed use and measured validity separate.

title: Prior work
text: This project is not the first to build on UK company data, and it deliberately reuses and benchmarks against what exists rather than starting from scratch. Investigative teams have used the PSC and Land Registry data to trace ownership (Global Witness, Private Eye and its successors, Transparency International UK); open-data organisations maintain standard-format ownership pipelines (Open Ownership, OpenSanctions); a long-running project links charities to companies (Find that Charity); and an academic literature studies small-company default and filing behaviour. Most of these are one-off investigations; a few maintain ongoing pipelines. The recurring lesson is that the genuine data advantage sits in the private layer none of them can rebuild — and that open, reproducible infrastructure is where there is still a real gap to fill.

What: analysis of Covid-era public contracts; found £15.3bn of high-risk contracts, with red flags including suppliers that were only weeks old (using incorporation dates).
For us: company age is a usable register signal. Source: the generated rule reference. (The deck slide suggested adding a company-age flag; this corrects it — one already exists, as context.)

What: open pipelines that convert UK PSC data into standard formats — Open Ownership’s bods-uk-psc-pipeline (Beneficial Ownership Data Standard) and OpenSanctions’ gb-coh-psc (now part of opensanctions/graph, FollowTheMoney format). Open Ownership has combined its output with procurement (Open Contracting) and sanctions data. A closely related applied study is Jofre & Knobel (2025), Insights from the United Kingdom’s People with Significant Control register.
For us: reuse these PSC pipelines and the standard formats; add sanctions links. These are maintained pipelines, not one-off investigations — the model to follow for the PSC work.



David Kane / 360Giving — Find that Charity

What: links 16 sources and ~660,000 non-profits; many charities are also companies and carry a company number. The same author wrote ixbrlparse, the library this project benchmarks its accounts parser against.
For us: charity lookup is already solved — reuse Find that Charity rather than building a charity join.



Academic research

What: a systematic review of 145 studies on predicting small-company default found nearly half used commercial data services. A 2024 study of 8,490 UK charitable companies found they file later when in financial difficulty (see also Clatworthy & Peel 2016 on private-company filing timeliness, in the evidence register).
For us: that so much of the default literature leans on paid data is exactly the gap an open, reproducible dataset can help fill — while being honest that filing behaviour is not, by itself, a validated predictor of fraud or insolvency.



Common tools, and the gap
Across these projects the recurring toolset is Jupyter and pandas, graph databases (Neo4j), Elasticsearch, linked data (RDF/SPARQL), and DuckDB. Most projects are one-off investigations; Open Ownership and OpenSanctions are the exceptions that maintain pipelines.

What it means for this project. None of this prior work can be rebuilt from Companies House alone where it depends on the private data layer (bank data, trade payments, judgments). The gap it can fill is open, documented, reproducible infrastructure over the free sources — which is the positioning of this whole project: explain and connect what exists, publish usable data, and add code only where it adds something.

title: Indicators: validation
text: Validation asks a narrow, honest question: when a company is independently known to have had an adverse insolvency event, does the pipeline’s corresponding flag fire? It compares cached pipeline flags against Insolvency Service adverse-case labels, using a control cohort of active companies matched on structural features (industry and age) that exist before any distress. Because the published labels contain positives but no verified negatives, this is a positive-unlabelled study: it can measure conditional recall and whether signals separate from a similar control, but it cannot establish precision, a false-positive rate, or anything about “trustworthiness”. No representative result is published yet.

title: Indicators: validation
text: Details

title: Indicators: validation
text:
Study design
The validation harness compares cached pipeline flags with Insolvency Service adverse-case labels. It is cache-only: sampling writes company-number lists, the operator fetches those lists explicitly, and evaluation then reads cached data. Recent positives are sampled because older labelled companies are often dissolved, purged, or recovered.
Conditional recall is the share of assessable labelled adverse companies for which the applicable insolvency signal fires. The denominator excludes records that cannot fairly be assessed, and every exclusion bucket is reported. Recall is also broken down by case type; solvent members’ voluntary liquidations do not count as adverse cases.
The primary result is the cohort disposition: how many labelled companies the current pipeline excludes as dissolved/closed, flags, misses, cannot find, or has not fetched. The positive cohort must be supplied explicitly during evaluation, preventing unrelated entries in the shared cache from entering the result. Conditional recall applies only to the currently screenable subset. Since the labels and register usually reflect the same filed insolvency event, high recall is expected and is not a predictive-performance claim.
The comparison cohort is drawn from active companies in the dated monthly snapshot and stratified to the positives by SIC section and coarse company-age band. Those are pre-distress structural confounders; downstream outcomes such as insolvency status, filing compliance, or charges are never matching dimensions.

title: Indicators: validation
text:
Positive-unlabelled framing
The label publication contains positives, not verified negatives. The control is therefore unlabelled and merely assumed not to be labelled positive. Its flag rate is not precision and is not a false-positive rate. The design can measure conditional recall and whether signals separate from a structurally similar control; it cannot establish accuracy against negative ground truth or validate the broader concept of trustworthiness.

text:
Details

Companies House describes its register as unverified information supplied by companies. ECCTA identity verification is rolling out and does not retrospectively verify all officer or PSC identities.
Officer/PSC same-person joins are fuzzy when based on names and partial dates of birth. Personal data remains local and is not published by this project.
Validation is positive-unlabelled: it measures conditional recall, not precision. The assumed-negative control has no negative ground truth.
Insolvency is an adjacent proxy for the broader and subjective idea of trustworthiness. Detecting insolvency does not validate trustworthiness, fraud, creditworthiness, or future solvency.
API current state, monthly snapshot state, and Insolvency Service labels from the 2012–2024 window are three distinct time bases. Apparent disagreement can reflect timing rather than a pipeline error.
Absence of a flag is weak evidence. Rules cover defined recorded facts and do not form a composite score or comprehensive due-diligence conclusion.

title: Who uses UK company data
text: The same free Companies House data flows outward to a wide range of users — and a striking amount of it flows straight back to the public sector as a packaged, scored product. Government buyers check suppliers’ financial health (often by buying credit-agency reports rather than reading raw filings); law enforcement, HMRC and the Insolvency Service use it in investigations; and official statistics draw on it. On the business side, credit agencies treat it as raw material, lenders and suppliers use it to set credit terms, and it underpins anti-money-laundering checks, sales prospecting, investment research and journalism. The pattern worth noticing: public data is paid for once to produce, given away free, and then bought back repackaged.

title: Who uses UK company data
text:
Details
Companies House’s own research identifies three user types: direct users (companies, creditors, investors, researchers), intermediaries (credit-reference agencies and other data providers that use it as an input), and providers of public goods (government departments and law enforcement). Source: deck slide 5 and notes (docs/source-material/companies-house-accounts-deck.md); the GOV.UK 2019 value study.

Public sector

Procurement. Cabinet Office guidance on assessing suppliers’ economic and financial standing expects buyers to check bidders’ financial health and monitor it during contracts — in practice, often by buying credit-agency reports rather than reading raw filings.
Law enforcement. A 2024 study estimated register value at around £2,600 per law-enforcement user per year (DBT/Companies House release, June 2025). [Estimated] (a study estimate).
Insolvency Service. Director-conduct and disqualification work draws on company filings — the same adverse records this project validates its indicators against.
Official statistics. The official business register used by ONS draws on administrative sources (presented generally here, not as a specific data-flow claim).
Local authorities checking suppliers and local businesses.



Business and others

Credit agencies and data providers — the raw material for their products.
Lenders and suppliers deciding credit terms.
Anti-money-laundering and know-your-customer checks: a 2024 study put the register’s value to AML-regulated businesses at £170–460m a year. [Estimated].
Sales prospecting, investors, researchers and journalists.


The point worth noticing. The same public data flows out for free, then gets bought back by the public sector as a packaged, scored product. Both Creditsafe and Dun & Bradstreet list services on the government’s G-Cloud Digital Marketplace. That mirrors the pattern in the GIS market, where most underlying data is open and much of the spend is on software and convenience — with one important exception (the private data layer) developed on the market page. Source: deck slide 5 notes; Digital Marketplace G-Cloud listings for Creditsafe and D&B Risk Analytics. [Checked] (listings exist).


What it means for you. If large, well-resourced buyers pay for packaging and convenience rather than for data they could get free, then an analyst at a smaller organisation can reproduce much of the descriptive layer from open data — which is exactly what this project does for the accounts. What you cannot reproduce is the private predictive layer; the market page is explicit about that boundary.

title: PSC / ownership (status)
text: Status: In progress. Reconnaissance of the PSC bulk snapshot is complete; the extractor is in design. No PSC dataset is published, and — by decision — only code will be, never the data. This page describes what the recon found and the design that follows from it.

title: PSC / ownership (status)
text:
Summary
“PSC” means persons with significant control — broadly, the people and entities that own or control a UK company. Companies House publishes a daily bulk snapshot of this register, and this project has analysed it end to end to decide what can responsibly be built from it. The short version: the snapshot is large (about 16 million records), it retains history back to 2016, and it is rich enough to support company-level ownership features — but it is personal data, it has no stable identifier for a person, and its internal structure is full of traps. So the plan is to publish code and company-level aggregates only, keep any person-level table private, and state match confidence honestly rather than imply a clean ownership graph.
This is deliberately a status page, not a dataset. It records the measured findings and the design decisions; it does not publish results.

title: PSC / ownership (status)
text:
Details

What the recon found
The recon ran over all 32 parts of the 2026-09-18 snapshot — 15,952,486 records, 0 bad lines, in 404 seconds, joined against the 2026-08-01 Basic Company Data (5,695,465 live companies). Every figure below traces to docs/recon-psc-results.md / docs/recon-psc-results.json; the full write-up is docs/recon-psc.md. [Checked] (project measurement).

History is reconstructable from 2016-04-06. Ceased PSC records are retained — 2,655,316 records (16.6%) carry a ceased_on date, and every notified-on year since 2016 keeps a ceased cohort. The product spans 10,917,257 distinct companies — nearly double the live register — so it holds PSC history for companies no longer live. 62,986 companies appear only as ceased records. Point-in-time control reconstruction is therefore feasible.
Statements exist, segregated at the tail. 922,564 records (5.8%) are persons-with-significant-control-statement records (e.g. “no PSC identified”), all in parts 31–32. The one-part probe that preceded the full recon wrongly concluded there were none — because parts 1–30 genuinely contain none.
Partitioning is meaningless. The ~32 parts are neither random samples nor company-number ranges — every part spans essentially the whole register, statements are segregated into 31–32, and recent years cluster in parts 25–30. No per-part rate is usable; stream all parts.
Composition. Individual PSCs 87.1%, corporate 6.7%, statements 5.8%, legal-person 0.1%, overseas-entity beneficial-owner variants ~0.3%, plus 545 super-secure records and 108 exemptions.
Individuals. Date of birth (year and month) present on 100%; identity-verification details on 50.6% (ECCTA rollout, start years 2025–2026); is_sanctioned present on 34,444, true on 17.
Corporate PSCs. A registration number is present on 91.0%, of which 77.9% resolve to a live company — a usable company-to-company ownership edge.
Natures of control. 35,169,887 assertions over 15,029,053 records; 55 distinct base rights once suffix families (-as-firm, -as-trust, -limited-liability-partnership, -registered-overseas-entity) are stripped.



Data-quality traps (document them before using)

No stable person ID. Linking the same person across companies is a fuzzy join. On a conservative key — (forename, surname, birth year, birth month) — 28.8% of keys appear on ≥2 records and 28.0% on ≥2 distinct companies: cross-company linkage is common, but the method’s confidence must be stated, not assumed. See person matching in pitfalls.
Dirty dates. 14,554 records have ceased_on before notified_on; 23,916 notified_on dates predate the 2016 regime (min 1083-01-01); 272 ceased_on dates fall outside 2016–2026 (269 before 2016; 3 after: 2924, 9998, 9999). 17,729 individuals imply an age under 16 at notification, 55 over 110. A cleaning rule is required before any time-series use. Source: docs/recon-psc-results.json (overall.ceased_on.years), corroborated by the loader’s f_ceased_out_of_range (see docs/AUDIT.md, “PSC loader Stage-1”). An earlier draft said 97, which was the 2016 ceased-date count (97,485) mis-transcribed. [Checked]
One-shot snapshot. Only today’s file is served; corrections over time are lost unless you archive snapshots yourself.



Design decisions that follow

Code only, never the data. PSC records are personal data, and users can download the snapshot directly from Companies House, so there is nothing to gain and real risk in republishing it. The repository will ship the extractor and methodology only. Source: docs/recon-psc.md, deck slide 17 notes.
Private person table, public per-company aggregates. Any person-level linkage table stays private. What could be published (as code producing them, not as a shipped dataset) are company-level features: PSC counts, corporate ownership chains, how many companies a person controls (with honest match confidence), and unresolved-ownership statement flags — none of which name an individual.
Nationality excluded. Nationality is present on 100% of individual records (4,666 distinct raw values) but is measured for data-quality documentation only and excluded from any product — a deliberate scope decision. Source: docs/recon-psc.md.
Honest match confidence. Because there is no stable person ID, any companies-per-person statistic is reported with its matching method and confidence, never as a settled fact.



Prior work to build on
This is well-trodden ground, and the plan is to reuse and benchmark against existing work rather than reinvent it (full summaries on the prior-work page):

Global Witness + DataKind UK, “The Companies We Keep” (2018) — matched people on name + birth month/year + address; the natural benchmark for this project’s person matching.
Open Ownership — its bods-uk-psc-pipeline publishes UK ownership in the Beneficial Ownership Data Standard, and has been combined with procurement and sanctions data.
OpenSanctions — its gb-coh-psc converter turns Companies House ownership data into a standard graph format.



Where to go next

How the sources join — where PSC sits among the UK sources.
Pitfalls — the PSC-specific traps (one-shot snapshots, person matching).
Prior work — what others have built with PSC data.

title: Accounts dataset: how we know it is right
text:
A dataset is only as useful as the reasons to trust it. This extractor was checked three ways. First, an accounting invariant: every fact read from a filing must land in exactly one category (kept, duplicate, conflict, skipped…) and the categories must sum to the total, so nothing is lost silently. Second, independent cross-checks: two separate implementations of the restatement calculation produced the same rate, and suspiciously round results flushed out two real bugs that are now covered by regression tests. Third, a parser comparison: the project’s own extractor was run head-to-head against two established tools — the ixbrlparse library and Arelle, a full standards-compliant XBRL processor — on real filings, with Arelle as the tie-breaker where the other two disagreed.
The headline is that on the numbers that actually get published, the project’s extractor agrees with ixbrlparse to 99.999%, while running about twelve times faster — and the comparison itself found and fixed three real bugs in the project’s own parser along the way.

title: Accounts dataset: how we know it is right
text:
Details






NoteParser check: complete



The parser-comparison chapter is finished; every figure on this page is one of its measured results, taken from committed files only. The headlines:

99.999% agreement on numeric facts with ixbrlparse — 119,812 of 119,813 shared numeric facts, 95% CI [99.995%, 100%]. Source: docs/accounts-parser-check.md, docs/accounts-validation-summary.md.
~12× faster than ixbrlparse, ~1,520× faster than Arelle — 0.65 vs 7.7 vs ~992 ms/filing. Source: docs/accounts-validation-summary.md, docs/accounts-parser-check.md.
Three real bugs found and fixed — the ix: prefix bug (61,085 filings recovered), comma-as-decimal formats (1,096 facts), and a hyphenated format name (540 facts); plus plain-XML support added (273,418 filings). Restatement rate unchanged at 9.36%. Source: docs/accounts-parser-check.md, docs/accounts-validation-summary.md.

[Checked] — every figure traces to the committed files named above.



1. The accounting invariant
Every tagged fact in a filing is assigned to exactly one disposition — kept, duplicate, conflict, skipped, and so on — and the per-category counts must add back up to the total facts read. If they don’t, the run fails rather than quietly dropping data. This is the project’s main defence against the failure mode it treats as the enemy: wrong-but-not-crashed. Source: deck slide 13 notes (docs/source-material/companies-house-accounts-deck.md).


2. Independent cross-checks

Two implementations, one answer. The restatement rate was computed by two separate engines (a Polars running-tally and an out-of-core DuckDB engine). On the 2022–2023 window they agreed at 7.93% vs 7.94%, matching an independent panel check — evidence the calculation is not an artefact of one implementation. Source: docs/accounts-restatement-2022-2023.md, deck slide 14.
Round numbers as a smoke alarm. Suspiciously round results (an exact 0% or 100%) exposed two real bugs during development; both are now covered by regression tests. Source: deck slide 13 notes.
Reconciliation and privacy guards. A full-corpus creditors reconciliation found zero sign-flip errors, and an automated staging guard re-scans every published Parquet against the personal-data lists before upload. Source: docs/accounts-creditors-maturity-reconciliation.md, docs/accounts-kaggle-safety-checks.md.



3. The parser comparison
Three parsers were run on the same fixed samples of real Companies House filings, under controlled timing (identical input, warm-up excluded, 3 repeats, median reported), with Arelle as the independent tie-breaker where ours and ixbrlparse disagreed. Source: docs/accounts-validation-summary.md, docs/accounts-parser-check.md.
Speed (5,000-filing fixed sample, end-to-end, 1 worker):

Projected to the full 35,806,258-filing archive at measured 8-worker throughput: ~2.1 h (ours) vs ~1.4 days (ixbrlparse) vs ~94.6 days (Arelle — not viable at this scale, so it serves as a referee on samples, not a production parser). [Checked] (measured; the full-archive figures are projections from the sample throughput — see docs/source-material/deck-corrections.md).
Accuracy: 99.999% agreement on numeric facts between ours and ixbrlparse (119,812 of 119,813 shared numeric facts; 95% CI [99.995%, 100%]; every year 2014–2026 individually at 99.9–100%). Dashes are excluded from this figure because both other parsers resolve a dash to zero immediately while this pipeline defers that to pivot time — the same published value, a design difference not a disagreement. An unfiltered, all-facts comparison shows 89.5% — most of that gap is a deliberate choice to keep non-numeric text as displayed rather than normalising it (e.g. “3 January 2023” vs “2023-01-03”), which never touches a numeric WIDE cell. Source: docs/accounts-validation-summary.md.

What it means for you. For the numbers WIDE actually publishes, the project’s fast extractor and a general-purpose library are effectively interchangeable in accuracy — the speed difference is what makes a full-archive, full-history build practical at all.



The 205-filing ONS tool check
A separate, reproducible check (the script is docs/source-material/tool-comparison-check.py) ran open-source tools over an ONS-curated sample of 379 real filings — 205 iXBRL and 174 plain XML (hand-picked, not random). It is the basis for the “reading a filing is solved” point:

(The ~33 ms/file here and the 7.7 ms/file in the speed table above are different samples and machines — both are reported with their context, not blended.) Two findings on this sample show what a parser cannot do for you: 164 concept/context pairs repeat within the filings (none disagree), and 99 of the 107 filings that report Creditors give only its parts, not a total. Source: docs/source-material/companies-house-accounts-notes.md, deck slide 12.


What the comparison found in our own parser
The exercise was not a victory lap — it found and fixed three real bugs:

Prefix bug — a hardcoded ix: namespace prefix silently extracted zero facts from any filing using a different binding. 61,085 filings recovered (measured directly; an earlier ~291,802 estimate was traced to a stale scan and corrected).
Comma-as-decimal formats — misread by ~100–1,000×; 1,096 facts corrected.
A hyphenated format name (num-dot-decimal) — silently nulled 540 facts across 3 months; found by tracing published values that disappeared between v1 and v2.
Plain-XML filings — 273,418 gained real facts via a new ixbrlparse adapter, verified against Arelle on 186 filings (100% agreement on shared facts).
Zero regressions; restatement rate unchanged at 9.36%; fill rates unchanged to within 0.3 percentage points.

Deferred by reasoned decision (documented, not hidden): nested facts (9.85% of filings but only 0.0015% of numeric facts and zero published columns) and text continuations (non-numeric only). Out of scope by design: multi-member and typed-member dimensional contexts (25.3% and 20.1% of filings, 37.9% combined). Source: docs/accounts-validation-summary.md, docs/accounts-limitations.md.

The honest framing. Good open-source parsers already exist; ixbrlparse does single-filing parsing well. What this project adds is the layer around it — full-history bulk orchestration, deduplication, totals-vs-parts rules, cross-filing restatement handling, point-in-time provenance, and a published table. The parsing was never the hard part; deciding which number is true, and when it was known, is. See the dataset and pitfalls.

title: Pitfalls we found, with examples
text:
Reading a single filing is a solved problem; turning millions of them into a trustworthy table is where the work is. Along the way this project hit a set of traps that are easy to miss and that change results quietly — a dash that means “nil” read as “missing”, a figure that appears twice because the prior year is restated, employee counts tagged in pounds, a mis-detected tag prefix that silently drops a whole filing. None of these crash anything; they just give you wrong numbers that look fine. This page lists each one with a concrete example and its effect on analysis, so you can check for them in your own work.
The failure mode this project treats as the enemy is wrong-but-not-crashed, not crashed. Each pitfall below is handled in the published datasets; they are documented here because the same traps apply to anyone building on this data from scratch.

title: Pitfalls we found, with examples
text:
Details
Each pitfall: what it is, a concrete example, and the effect on analysis. Sources are named inline; the fullest treatment of each is in the docs/accounts-*.md files and docs/AUDIT.md.

1. A dash means nil, not missing
UK accounts print “–” for a nil value. If a parser reads that dash as missing, a later filing’s comparative can quietly fill the gap — a look-ahead leak.

Example: a 2020 filing reports Debtors — (genuinely nil). Read as missing, a 2021 filing that restates 2020 debtors as £4,000 can back-fill the 2020 cell with a value that was not known at the time.
Effect: both pivot engines now coalesce a dash to 0 so it competes normally. Diffed cell-by-cell, this changed 1,936,525 WIDE cells under as_first_reported (1,936,433 null→0, 92 real-value→0). Source: docs/accounts-dash-nil-fix.md, docs/accounts-limitations.md.



2. Comparatives and restatements
Every filing contains the current year and a prior-year comparative, so the same (company, period, concept) appears in more than one filing — and the two values do not always agree.

Example: a company’s 2020 accounts report equity of £50,000 for 2020; its 2021 accounts, which restate 2020 as a comparative, show £48,000. Same period, two values.
Effect: 9.36% of repeated (company, period, concept) keys disagree with the first-reported value across 2014–2026 — and it is not flat by year (keys first reported in 2016–2017 restate 13–15%, the rest of the span 8–10%). For any predictive work use the as-first-reported values; the latest values incorporate figures that postdate the period and leak the future. Source: docs/accounts-restatement-2014-2026.md, docs/accounts-restatement-by-year.md, docs/accounts-limitations.md.



3. Creditors is given only as parts
Most filers report creditors by maturity, not as a single total — and even when a bare total is filed, it is often not a genuine sum.

Example: a filing reports creditors due within one year = £30,000 and after one year = £10,000 but no combined Creditors line; another files a Creditors total that turns out to equal just the within-one-year bucket.
Effect: the bare Creditors total is only about 4% populated (3.82% in the published file), and where a total is filed alongside the split, 80.3% of such cases equal just the WithinOneYear bucket rather than a real total. Use creditors_within_one_year and creditors_after_one_year, not Creditors. Source: docs/accounts-limitations.md, docs/accounts-creditors-maturity-reconciliation.md.



4. Employee counts tagged in pounds
The average-employees figure is sometimes tagged with a currency unit instead of a plain count.

Example: <ix:nonFraction name="AverageNumberEmployeesDuringPeriod" unitRef="GBP">3 — a headcount of 3, mis-labelled as £3.
Effect: about 29% of employee facts carry a GBP unit; the median such value is 1.0, so almost all are real headcounts with the wrong label, with a small tail of genuine monetary values (e.g. staff costs). Do not filter employees by unit or you silently lose ~29% of coverage. The dataset keeps every value as filed and sets employees_unit_anomaly = 1 on affected rows. Employee coverage also has a 2020–2021 reporting-regime break — an apparent jump or gap across that boundary may be an artefact. Source: docs/accounts-employee-unit-cutoff.md, docs/accounts-limitations.md.



5. Scale and sign (and European number formats)
An iXBRL numeric tag carries a sign and, via its format, a number convention. Ignore them and the magnitude or direction is wrong.

Example: a fact with format="ixt2:numdotcomma" and text 4.506 means 4,506, not 4.506 — the dot is a thousands separator. A sign="-" attribute makes the value negative even though the printed digits look positive.
Effect: comma-as-decimal formats (numdotcomma/numcomma/numspacecomma/ numcommadecimal) were misread by roughly 100–1,000× until fixed — 1,096 facts changed value archive-wide (e.g. a real CashBankOnHand fact read as 3.349 instead of 3349). In the independent ONS tool check, all 363 sign="-" figures were handled correctly by ixbrlparse. Source: docs/accounts-validation-summary.md, docs/source-material/deck-corrections.md, docs/source-material/tool-comparison-check.py.



6. Namespace prefixes
iXBRL tags live in a namespace that a filing can bind to any prefix. Hardcode one prefix and you silently drop every filing that uses another.

Example: the extractor matched ix:nonFraction, but a filing binding inline-XBRL to a different prefix (or the default namespace) — e.g. <ixbrli:nonFraction> — matched nothing, so that filing extracted zero facts and simply vanished from the data without error.
Effect: fixing the prefix detection recovered 61,085 filings (measured directly; concentrated 2014–2022). An earlier sample-based estimate of ~291,802 was wrong because it was computed from stale scan files — corrected to the measured figure. Source: docs/accounts-validation-summary.md, docs/source-material/deck-corrections.md.



7. Plain-XML filings
A small tail of filings are plain XBRL (.xml), not iXBRL (.html). An extractor built only for the HTML form skips them entirely.

Example: a monthly archive contains mostly .html iXBRL plus a minority of .xml filings; the XML ones were previously dropped, so early-year coverage looked thinner than it was.
Effect: plain-XML filings are 301,141 archive-wide (0.84%); they are now read through an ixbrlparse-based adapter (273,418 gained real facts), verified against Arelle on 186 filings (100% agreement on shared facts). The share is larger in early years, so check it before trusting 2014–2018 coverage. Source: docs/accounts-validation-summary.md, docs/accounts-limitations.md.



8. One-shot PSC snapshots
The PSC product is a daily snapshot, not an event stream — only today’s file is served.

Example: a PSC’s details are corrected between two days; unless you archived yesterday’s snapshot, the pre-correction state is gone.
Effect: to reconstruct history you must archive snapshots yourself. The good news: ceased PSC records are retained, so control history is reconstructable from 2016-04-06 (the product spans 10,917,257 distinct companies — nearly double the live register). The bad news: the ~32 parts are not random samples or company-number ranges (statements are segregated into parts 31–32; recent years cluster in parts 25–30), so no per-part rate is usable — stream all parts. Source: docs/recon-psc.md, docs/recon-psc-results.md.



9. Person matching with no stable ID
PSC and officer records have no stable person identifier, so linking the same person across companies is a fuzzy join.

Example: the same individual appears as a PSC of several companies with slightly different name spellings and addresses; matching on (forename, surname, birth year, birth month) collides real people and splits one person across variants.
Effect: on a conservative key, 28.8% of person-keys appear on two or more records and 28.0% on two or more distinct companies — so cross-company linkage is common, but the method’s confidence must be stated, not assumed. Global Witness/DataKind matched on name + birth month/year + address; this project will benchmark its matching against theirs. Source: docs/recon-psc-results.md, prior work.


What it means for you. If you build on this data directly, test for each of these before trusting a result: a nil read as missing, a restated comparative, a creditors total that is really one bucket, employees filtered by unit, an ignored scale/sign, a dropped filing from a prefix mismatch, skipped XML, an un-archived PSC snapshot, and an over-confident person join. The published accounts dataset handles the accounts ones for you; the validation page shows how each fix was checked.

title: How the UK sources join
text:
Companies House is not the only free UK source of company data — it is the spine that the others attach to. The Gazette, HM Land Registry, payment-practices reports, public-procurement records, charity registers, the overseas-entities register and the FCA register each add a different column to the same picture, and most of them join to a company on its company number. The catch is rarely price: most of these are free. The catch is licences (some forbid republishing) and matching (some sources carry the company number cleanly, others only sometimes). This page lists each source with what it adds, how it joins, how to get it, whether it can be republished, its known problems, who has used it before, and where this project stands on it.
A second, blunter point sits underneath the map: some of the most predictive data cannot be got this way at all. Bank-credit behaviour, trade-payment histories and court judgments are private or paid, and no amount of open-data engineering reconstructs them. That boundary is set out at the end.

title: How the UK sources join
text:
Details
Each source below joins to Companies House mostly on the company number. “Our status” uses four values: Done, In progress, Planned, Not planned. Match-quality and access claims carry a [Checked] / [Estimated] label; everything traces to deck slides 6–8 and their notes (docs/source-material/companies-house-accounts-deck.md and companies-house-accounts-notes.md), the project plan (docs/plan.md), the README, and the literature queue (literature/open-company-uk-source-queue-2026-08.md).

Companies House itself
Companies House is several sources in one. Treat each product separately.
Register (Basic Company Data)

What it adds: the spine — name, number, status, registered office, SIC codes, incorporation and accounts-due dates for every live company.
Join key / match: the company number is the key. [Checked]
Access & licence: free monthly CSV; OGL v3.0, republishable (personal data aside).
Known problems: live companies only, no history — reconstructing past states means keeping your own monthly copies.
Our status: Done — used as population context and the stratification spine in the indicator validation.

Accounts bulk data

What it adds: the actual financial figures — balance-sheet items, employee counts — tagged in iXBRL/XML. See the accounts guide.
Join key / match: company number, inside each filing. [Checked]
Access & licence: free daily/monthly ZIPs back to 2008; OGL v3.0. The financial facts are not personal data, so a derived financials dataset can be published.
Known problems: electronically filed only; mostly balance sheets; the API returns no parsed numbers, so you must parse the filings yourself.
Our status: Done — the published 2014–2026 accounts dataset.

PSC (persons with significant control)

What it adds: ownership and control — who owns or controls each company, and declared statements where no PSC is identified.
Join key / match: company number; person-level linkage is fuzzy (no stable person ID — see the PSC page). [Checked]
Access & licence: free daily JSON snapshot; OGL v3.0, but it contains personal data, so this project publishes code only.
Known problems: only today’s snapshot is served; corrections over time are lost unless you archive. One-shot snapshot, not an event log.
Our status: In progress — recon complete, extractor in design.

Officers (directors and secretaries)

What it adds: who runs the company; appointment/resignation history; ECCTA identity verification fields.
Join key / match: company number via the API; person linkage is fuzzy. [Checked]
Access & licence: the bulk officers product is on request only, not a public download; the per-company API is free. Personal data — code only.
Our status: Done (via API, in the indicator pipeline) — officer churn and identity-verification attributes are derived per company; the bulk product is Not planned.

APIs (REST / Streaming / Document)

What it adds: current, per-company state and the filed documents themselves.
Access & licence: free key; rate-limited (~600 req/5min per key, [Not verified] — see Companies House guide).
Known problems: no parsed financial figures; no bulk history.
Our status: Done — the indicator pipeline is API-first for freshness-sensitive state.



The Gazette

What it adds: official insolvency and strike-off notices with dates — winding-up petitions, liquidations, strike-offs. Good for outcome labels and, more usefully, timing: how far ahead of a winding-up petition does a register or accounts signal appear?
Join key / match: company number present in notices. [Checked]
Access & licence: free official API (JSON), paged; free web viewing is OGL. A separate commercial Data Service exists — investigate a reproducible open acquisition route before planning ingestion.
Known problems: separate the free OGL route from the paid Data Service.
Prior work: Transparency International UK used incorporation dates and notices as red flags (see prior work).
Our status: Planned — the next specified external integration (docs/plan.md, README).



HM Land Registry — company property ownership

What it adds: which UK and overseas companies own property in England & Wales — asset ownership, and a bridge to overseas owners.
Join key / match: company registration number. [Checked]
Access & licence: free monthly CSV (free since November 2017, account and licence required), historical files via API. The licence does not allow republishing — so, as with PSC, publish code only.
Known problems: republishing restriction; coverage is England & Wales.
Prior work: Private Eye (2015) → Who Owns England → TaxPolicy.org.uk (January 2026), which cross-checked Land Registry against the overseas-entities register and published its method.
Our status: Planned.



Payment-practices reporting

What it adds: the only open signal on payment behaviour — large firms’ average days to pay, share of invoices paid late, and standard terms. This is the open stand-in for the trade-payment data credit agencies sell privately.
Join key / match: company number on every report. [Checked]
Access & licence: all reports downloadable; open.
Known problems: large companies only — it does not cover the small/micro majority.
Our status: Planned.



Contracts Finder / Find a Tender

What it adds: public contracts and winning suppliers — public-sector exposure, and very new suppliers winning contracts (a documented red flag).
Join key / match: sometimes — supplier identifiers are inconsistent, so matching needs work. [Estimated] (contract→company-number match quality is not yet measured here).
Access & licence: bulk, Open Contracting Data Standard; open.
Prior work: Transparency International UK (“Track and Trace”, “Behind the Masks”); Open Ownership has combined PSC with procurement data.
Our status: Planned.



Charity registers (Charity Commission, OSCR, CCNI)

What it adds: the non-profit segment — many charities are also companies and carry a company number; finances and trustees.
Join key / match: mostly — most charitable companies carry a company number. [Estimated].
Access & licence: bulk downloads; open.
Prior work: David Kane / 360Giving’s Find that Charity already links 16 sources and ~660,000 non-profits (the same author wrote ixbrlparse).
Our status: Not planned as an own build — reuse Find that Charity if a charity join is needed.



Register of Overseas Entities
